dropped_question.title: Does BitNet b1.58 use only additions for matrix multiplication in practice?
dropped_question.question_body: The paper says matrix multiplications involve almost no multiplications, relying on integer additions because weights are in {−1, 0, +1}. For a dot-product \(y = \sum_i w_i x_i\) with ternary \(w_i\), we still need to implement \(w_i x_i\) as \(+x_i\), \(0\), or \(-x_i\). On current GPUs/CPUs, isn't this still implemented with integer multiply-accumulate instructions or table/bit operations? Can you clarify what kernels or primitives are used so that actual multiplication is avoided and whether popcount-style tricks are utilized?

equivalent_probe: Which arithmetic operation's elimination primarily explains BitNet's dramatic energy savings during matrix multiplication?
explanation: The generated question is fundamentally asking whether multiplications are actually avoided in practice and what primitives replace them. That maps to the same core point as the probe: the paper's energy savings come from eliminating multiply operations in matrix multiplications (replacing them with sign/zero-selection and additions or bitwise/popcount-style tricks). Both questions focus on the removal/avoidance of multiplication as the key change driving savings.

dropped_question.title: Is the quantization function equivalent to a form of weight normalization or L1 regularization?
dropped_question.question_body: Because weights are divided by \(\gamma = \mathrm{absmean}(W)\) before rounding to {−1,0,+1}, this resembles a kind of normalization. Does this implicitly impose a regularization effect similar to weight normalization or an \(\ell_1\) penalty? Is there a theoretical link explaining why introducing 0 improves "feature filtering" and generalization?

equivalent_probe: What is the conceptual role of gamma in the weight quantization formula?
explanation: Both questions ask for the same conceptual understanding of the absmean scaling (gamma) used before rounding. The generated question queries whether dividing weights by gamma is a form of normalization or imposes an L1-like regularization; the probe asks for the conceptual role of gamma in the quantization formula. They seek the same explanation of gamma's purpose (a scale/normalization factor that sets thresholds for discretization), so they are semantically equivalent.

dropped_question.title: How do you prevent accuracy loss from quantizing activations symmetrically without zero-point?
dropped_question.question_body: The paper removes zero-point quantization by symmetrically scaling activations to \([-Q_b, Q_b]\). Many quantization schemes benefit from asymmetric quantization with a zero-point, especially for non-symmetric distributions. Why is symmetric sufficient here, and did you measure the difference in perplexity/accuracy between symmetric vs asymmetric activation quantization?

equivalent_probe: What implicit assumption about token activations justifies the claim that per-token scaling to [-Q_b, Q_b] causes negligible performance change?
explanation: Both questions ask the same core thing: why per-token symmetric scaling of activations into [-Q_b, Q_b] (i.e., removing an explicit zero-point/asymmetric offset) does not meaningfully hurt model quality. The generated question asks why symmetric quantization without a zero-point is sufficient and whether symmetric vs asymmetric quantization was measured; the probe asks for the implicit assumption that justifies the claim that per-token symmetric scaling causes negligible performance change. Both target the same conceptual justification (and implicit empirical comparison) for using symmetric activation quantization instead of asymmetric quantization with a zero-point.

dropped_question.title: Does the inclusion of zero in the ternary set explicitly improve "feature filtering"?
dropped_question.question_body: The paper claims modeling capability is stronger because weights can be 0, enabling explicit feature filtering. Do you have evidence (e.g., sparsity patterns or ablations) showing that zero weights tend to prune redundant channels/features and improve downstream accuracy compared to purely binary {−1, +1} weights?

equivalent_probe: If BitNet b1.58 reverted to only {-1, 1} weights (no zero), which modeling capability would be most directly lost?
explanation: Both questions target the same core claim: that allowing a weight value of 0 enables explicit feature filtering/pruning (i.e., turning off redundant channels) and thus affects modeling capability/accuracy compared to a purely binary {-1,+1} scheme. The generated question asks for empirical evidence of this pruning/accuracy benefit, while the probe asks which capability would be lost without 0; both are essentially probing the same conclusion—that the 0 state enables feature filtering and its removal degrades that ability.
